name: afsctool
desc: Utility for manipulating APFS and ZFS compressed files
why: Exposes APFS and HFS compression internals on macOS, a close call but a real look at filesystem compression.

brief.what_it_is: afsctool is a command-line utility for macOS that applies Apple File System Compression to files, decompresses files that are already compressed, or reports information about compressed files. The original blog describes it as working on HFS+ compression on Mac OS 10.6 or later. This GitHub fork (RJVB/afsctool) also covers APFS, adds LZVN and LZFSE support, and builds a second executable, zfsctool. Input is one or more file or folder paths on the command line, and output is compression statistics or the compressed or decompressed files on disk.
brief.why_it_exists: The blog post frames it as a way to use AFSC (Apple File System Compression) on existing files, which the author says Finder does not let you do directly. The blogger's own example is compressing a large World of Warcraft install, and a commenter reports running it nightly as a cron job over ~/Library mail and sync directories to save SSD space.
brief.how_it_works: Per the fork README, afsctool compresses files by writing them back in compressed form, with an undo path if something goes wrong and an optional backup while compressing. Parallel modes -j and -J let you set a worker-thread count; -j parallelises only the compression step while disk I/O runs with exclusive access, and -J parallelises all steps. zfsctool takes a different route: ZFS compression is set per dataset, so it recompresses by changing the dataset's compression property, rewriting the files, and resetting the property, which also affects other files written during the rewrite.

commands_seen.context: From the blog comments: compress a single large file with -c (compress) and -v (verbose). The reported result was 'Unable to compress file.'

brief.install_notes: Build from source with CMake; there is no brew formula described in the README. You need zlib (1.2.8 or newer), Google's sparsehash, cmake and pkgconfig, installed through MacPorts, Fink, or Homebrew. Clone with --recurse-submodules so the lzfse submodule is present. With Homebrew you must set PKG_CONFIG_PATH by hand. zfsctool needs only a runtime dependency on ZFS (OpenZFS on OS X).
brief.standout: The parallel modes are unusual for this kind of tool: -j and -J let you pick the worker count, and -S with -R can compress the largest files first to limit free-space fragmentation. zfsctool is also an interesting idea, since it recompresses ZFS data by flipping a dataset's compression property and rewriting, a workaround for ZFS having no API to get or set that property.
brief.status: unknown. The blog's latest version is 1.6.4 (build 34), and the fork README covers up to 1.7.2 with a mention of 1.7.1 and 1.7.2 changes, but I saw no release dates or commit dates in either page. The fork README also says zfsctool 'doesn't yet do anything except for printing out statistics', which suggests active but early work.
brief.caveats: macOS only, Mac OS 10.6 or later. Building from source requires several dependencies and CMake, and the README gives no prebuilt download. The blog's download link URL did not come through, so I could not confirm the official binary. LZVN support in the fork needs the lzfse submodule, and the README says LZFSE decompression 'should work' but is not confirmed. The README says the permission-change feature for read-only files has 'No error checking'. zfsctool is a work in progress that only prints statistics. The blog's version history ends at 1.6.4, so the fork's extra features are not in the homepage's release. I took the fork URL from a guess at the upstream repository location, since the homepage did not link to it.

judge.reason: A niche filesystem tool that lets you inspect and apply Apple’s otherwise-hidden file compression offers a worthwhile peek into how APFS stores data.

entry.title: afsctool
entry.tldr: A macOS command-line tool that applies, removes, and reports Apple's transparent filesystem compression on files Finder won't compress for you.
entry.deeper_look:
afsctool takes file or folder paths and either compresses them with Apple File System Compression, decompresses files that already use it, or prints statistics about what is compressed. The compression is transparent: files look and behave the same to applications, but take less space on disk. The original blog post describes it as working with HFS+ compression on Mac OS 10.6 or later. The RJVB fork, which is the README the brief was built from, adds APFS, LZVN and LZFSE support, and a second executable called zfsctool.

The author's stated motive is that Finder gives you no way to compress existing files this way. The blog's own example is a large World of Warcraft install. One commenter reports running it nightly from cron over mail and sync directories in ~/Library to save SSD space.

Per the fork README, it compresses by writing each file back in compressed form, with an undo path if something goes wrong and an optional backup. The -j and -J flags set a worker-thread count. -j parallelises only the compression step while disk I/O runs with exclusive access, and -J parallelises every step. Combining -S with -R compresses the largest files first, which limits free-space fragmentation.

zfsctool is the odd idea here. ZFS compression is set per dataset and there is no API to get or set it per file, so it recompresses by changing the dataset's compression property, rewriting the files, then resetting the property. That also affects other files written during the rewrite. It is a door into how filesystems store compressed data, and how much of it is hidden from ordinary tools.
entry.install:
brew install afsctool
# macOS only. The brief's README describes a CMake source build (needs zlib 1.2.8+, google-sparsehash, cmake, pkgconfig, and git clone --recurse-submodules). zfsctool needs OpenZFS on OS X at runtime.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the usage text and the list of flags.
Prints usage for the ZFS companion tool.
Compresses one large file verbosely. In a blog comment this particular run reported 'Unable to compress file.' so expect some files to refuse.

entry.whats_unique: It exposes Apple's built-in transparent compression, which Finder doesn't offer on existing files, and adds parallel compression modes. zfsctool tries the same trick on ZFS by flipping a dataset property and rewriting.
entry.caveats: macOS only. Maintenance status is unclear, the brief found no release or commit dates, and zfsctool is early work that only prints statistics.
